title: 3 High-Yielding Stocks That Performed Well During the Last Market Crash - The Globe and Mail
content: AbbVie, Chevron, and Coca-Cola have excellent fundamentals and pay relatively high dividends. During the last market crash in 2022, all these stocks did reasonably well, with total returns that were into double digits. Given the shakiness around the S&P 500 these days and the volatility around Nvidia and other leading tech companies, there's a growing fear that the market may be heading for a crash, especially with interest rates looking like they will rise again next month. Even a hot new IPO such as Anthropic is struggling in its early trading days. The excitement around the once-hot stock market appears to be fading. The good news, however, is that investors don't have to exit the market, even if they're worried about a potential market crash. Some stocks may be safe investments to hang on to, even during a downturn in the markets. Missed AI’s "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 15x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we’re only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » Three stocks that did well during the most recent crash in 2022 were AbbVie (NYSE:ABBV), Chevron (NYSE:CVX), and Coca-Cola (NYSE:KO). Here's how they did back when the S&P 500 fell by 19%, and why they can be resilient investments to hang on to for the long haul. Healthcare can be a reasonably stable sector of the market to invest in for the long haul. That's because top healthcare companies sell medicines and devices that are essential for patients and hospitals, helping insulate their financials from otherwise adverse economic conditions. AbbVie isn't a terribly fast-growing business, but it is a diverse one. In its most recent quarter, which ended on Sept. 30, it generated organic growth of around 11%. Its business is broad, with multiple products in immunology, neuroscience, oncology, and aesthetics contributing to its top line. Many of its medications delivered growth in excess of 20% in its most recent quarter. On top of that solid growth, it also pays a dividend that yields 2.4%, which is more than double the rate of the S&P 500 average. Back in 2022, AbbVie's stock generated total returns (which include dividends) of just over 24%. With the stock still trading at a reasonable 18 times its estimated future profits (based on analyst expectations), it remains an excellent buy right now. Oil and gas giant Chevron can be a solid option to consider when stocks are struggling due to inflation, as they were in 2022. Inflation sent oil prices up to levels not seen in years, and Chevron was a big winner, raking in massive profits. As a leading producer, the company is in excellent shape to take advantage of such opportunities in the oil and gas sector. Unsurprisingly, as oil prices took off in 2022, so did Chevron's share price, with its total returns coming at 58%. This year, with oil prices once again on the rise due to the war in Iran, it's up around 38%. A big incentive to buy the stock is its dividend. Not only does it yield around 3.5%, but Chevron has been increasing it for decades. This can be an excellent income stock to hang on to for safety and as a hedge against adverse market conditions. Coca-Cola is a name that, in the investing world, is known for its rock-solid stability. It's a stock that billionaire investor Warren Buffett is a fan of due to its strong fundamentals, excellent brand, and the simplicity of its business. It's a company whose products are largely going to remain in demand regardless of economic cycles, as they aren't extremely expensive and are staples in grocery stores. What's impressive about the business is that despite rising competition, its margins remain incredibly healthy. Over the past four quarters, Coca-Cola's net profit of $14.8 billion was nearly 30% of its revenue, which totaled $51.1 billion over that time frame. It's a sign of the brand's strength that Coca-Cola doesn't need to lower prices in order to generate sales growth. In 2022, the stock's total returns were a little under 11%. While those are the lowest returns on the list, the stock still did far better than the overall market. At 2.2%, Coca-Cola's yield has come down this year due to its rising share price. However, with the company raising its dividend for 64 consecutive years, it's another excellent investment to hold for the long haul. The narrative fair value of AbbVie at $310 sits above the last close at $286.20, which frames the oncology push inside a wider story about cash generation and concentration risk. According to IamPotato, an investor in the Simply Wall St Community who wrote the narrative, the key question is how long the current immunology engine can carry the rest of the portfolio. AbbVie has largely completed one of the most closely watched product transitions in pharmaceuticals. Skyrizi and Rinvoq have more than offset the steep decline in Humira, driving double-digit revenue growth and allowing the company to raise full-year guidance. The near-term picture is strong, but the portfolio is now heavily concentrated on these two immunology assets, and longer-term patent and competitive risks remain. title: Could $1,000 a Month in Dividend Stocks Make You Rich by 2040? - The Globe and Mail

At their five-year growth rates, $1,000 a month in Enterprise Products Partners, AbbVie, or Alphabet would grow to roughly $414,000 to $924,000 by 2040. Reaching $1 million in 14 years requires extraordinary returns, so most investors are better off building wealth over decades. Some investors thumb their noses at dividends because they're not interested in income. That's a mistake. Since 1926, more than 30% of the S&P 500's (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) total return has come from reinvesting dividends. Granted, the percentage has been lower in recent years (due to the index's strong growth). However, dividends are an important component of wealth growth. That raises a question, though: Can you become wealthy investing solely in dividend stocks? Let's narrow the question even further. Could investing $1,000 a month in dividend stocks make you rich by 2040? Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again.In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » Before we can answer that question, we must first address another critical one: How much money does it take to be rich? Different people will respond differently to that question. The Barenaked Ladies tackled the question in 1992. The title of their song "If I Had a Million Dollars" gives away their answer: a cool $1 million. Many Americans might still agree that having $1 million would qualify a person as rich. However, inflation has eroded the buying power of a dollar (or 1 million of them) over the last 34 years. Charles Schwab's (NYSE:SCHW) 2025 Modern Wealth Survey found that a net worth of $2.3 million was the threshold for being wealthy. But to be financially comfortable, the average response was $839,000. Answers varied considerably by region, though. Let's go with The Barenaked Ladies' number for calculation purposes. Let's also use three very different dividend stocks to determine whether investing $1,000 per month could grow to $1 million by 2040. Enterprise Products Partners(NYSE:EPD) ranks among the most attractive ultra-high-yield dividend stocks. The pipeline stock pays a distribution yield of around 6.3%. Enterprise has increased its distribution for 28 consecutive years. It's remarkably resilient, generating strong cash flow even during the financial crisis of 2008 and 2009 and the COVID-19 pandemic. This midstream energy company has delivered a total return compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of roughly 19% over the past five years. What would buying $1,000 per month of Enterprise Products Partners' units (limited partnerships have units rather than shares) be worth after 14 years at that rate? Around $724,000. That's enough to make many Americans feel financially comfortable, but it's still well below our $1 million threshold to be rich. Maybe turning to dividend royalty would get us closer to reaching the goal. AbbVie (NYSE:ABBV) has increased its dividend for an impressive 53 consecutive years, earning it a spot among the Dividend Kings -- a group of stocks with 50 or more consecutive years of dividend growth. The big drugmaker has successfully navigated a patent cliff and markets multiple blockbuster drugs. AbbVie's forward dividend yield is slightly north of 2.5%, which is lower than historical levels primarily because the pharma stock has performed well. As a result, AbbVie's total return CAGR over the last five years is around 22%. If you bought $1,000 of the stock each month through 2040, you'd have almost $924,000 at that growth rate. We wouldn't quite reach the $1 million mark, but we'd be closer with AbbVie than with Enterprise Products Partners. What if we focused more on growth than dividends? Google parent Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG)(NASDAQ:GOOGL) pays a minuscule dividend yield of 0.33%. However, the company is a leader in several key technologies shaping the future, including artificial intelligence (AI), cloud services, driverless cars, and quantum computing. You might think all of this would be enough to vault Alphabet well past Enterprise Products Partners and AbbVie. However, that's not the case. Over the last five years, Alphabet's total return CAGR was around 12% -- a respectable but not jaw-dropping number. Investing $1,000 per month in the stock through 2040 at this CAGR would give you less than $414,000 at the end of the 14 years. So what's the answer to our initial question? Investing $1,000 a month in dividend stocks could make you rich by 2040 (with "rich" defined as $1 million), but you would need to find stocks that deliver extraordinarily high total returns. That's easier said than done. None of the three stocks we evaluated would have achieved the goal. Note, too, that the calculations above assumed that Enterprise Products Partners, AbbVie, and Alphabet would continue to grow at the same rate as they have over the past five years. That may or may not be the case. There's another approach, though, that could be better for most investors. Don't worry about becoming rich in 14 years; focus on growing your wealth over the long term -- multiple decades. With a diversified portfolio of solid dividend stocks, that goal should be attainable.
